slides.title: Lesson outline
bullets: Tests: Prostate-specific antigen (PSA); Carcinoembryonic antigen (CEA); Alpha-fetoprotein (AFP) tumor marker; CA-125 (cancer antigen 125); CA 19-9 (cancer antigen 19-9)

slides.title: Prostate-specific antigen (PSA)
slides.eyebrow: Tumor markers · What it is used for · 1/2
bullets: Specimen: Venous blood  ·  Units: ng/mL

What it is used for: The PSA test is used to monitor diagnosed prostate cancer and its treatment, to follow up prostate symptoms (painful or frequent urination, blood in urine or semen, pelvic and/or back pain), to screen men without symptoms for prostate cancer, and to help diagnose prostate conditions that are not cancer.

Per NCI, PSA is not recommended for routine screening of the general population; most organizations advise discussing benefits and harms with a doctor first. The US Preventive Services Task Force (USPSTF) says that at 55–69 the decision is individual and that PSA screening is not recommended at 70 and older. Some organizations recommend routine testing from age 40 or 45 for people at higher risk (for example, a father or brother with prostate cancer, inherited BRCA2/BRCA1 variants). Risk rises after age 50.

slides.title: Prostate-specific antigen (PSA)
slides.eyebrow: Tumor markers · What it is used for · 2/2
bullets: Physiology: PSA is a protein made by both normal and malignant cells of the prostate — a gland of the male reproductive system just below the bladder that makes the fluid part of semen. A low level of PSA in blood is normal.

slides.title: Prostate-specific antigen (PSA)
bullets: High: Causes of a high PSA include prostate cancer, an enlarged prostate (benign prostatic hyperplasia), prostatitis (inflammation of the gland), other prostate problems, urinary tract infections and certain medicines. The test cannot show the cause, so further tests may be needed: a repeat PSA, a digital rectal exam, a urine test for infection, a prostate biopsy. Only a biopsy can diagnose cancer.

High: If a screening PSA is high in someone without symptoms, the doctor may repeat the PSA in 6–8 weeks to confirm it. If it stays high — observation with repeat PSA tests and digital rectal exams; if it keeps rising (especially quickly) or a lump is felt — more blood or urine tests, imaging such as MRI, or a biopsy.

slides.title: Prostate-specific antigen (PSA)
bullets: High: After surgery or radiation for prostate cancer, a rising PSA may be the first sign of recurrence (a “biochemical relapse”), often months or years before symptoms. But a single high value does not always mean recurrence — the doctor looks for a rising trend over time.

slides.title: Prostate-specific antigen (PSA)
bullets: Pre-analytics: Ejaculation can raise PSA: MedlinePlus advises avoiding sex and masturbation for 24 hours before the test, while NCI advises avoiding activities that may raise PSA for 2 days before testing — ask your provider for the exact interval. Tell the provider about medicines you take, but do not stop them on your own.

Interferences: Prostate infection or inflammation and a recent biopsy can raise PSA for a month or two; vigorous exercise (such as cycling) and ejaculation raise it briefly. Finasteride and dutasteride, used for an enlarged prostate, lower PSA — a lower cutoff is used for people taking them.

slides.title: Prostate-specific antigen (PSA)
bullets: Limitations: There is no single threshold that separates a normal from an abnormal PSA. The higher the PSA, the more likely cancer is, but a high PSA without cancer and a low PSA with cancer are both possible. Per NCI, a level above 4.0 ng/mL is generally considered abnormal and may lead to a biopsy recommendation; but because PSA rises with age, some doctors use a higher cutoff (e.g., 5 ng/mL) for older men and a lower one (e.g., 2.5 ng/mL) for younger men.

Possible harms of screening: false positives are common — about 6%–7% of men per screening round, and only about 25% of men biopsied for an elevated PSA are found to have cancer. Biopsy can cause bleeding, infection and pain. Finding slow-growing cancers that would never cause harm (overdiagnosis) can lead to unneeded treatment and its complications — erectile dysfunction, urinary or bowel incontinence.

slides.title: Prostate-specific antigen (PSA)
bullets: General rule: circulating tumor markers have generally not worked well for screening people without symptoms — they miss some cancers (not sensitive enough) and can suggest cancer in people who do not have it (not specific enough). Non-cancer conditions can raise a marker, and some cancers do not raise it. A high marker only means cancer is more likely; a biopsy is usually needed to diagnose or rule out cancer.

slides.title: Carcinoembryonic antigen (CEA)
slides.eyebrow: Tumor markers · What it is used for
bullets: Specimen: Usually venous blood; less often cerebrospinal, chest or abdominal (peritoneal) fluid

What it is used for: CEA testing is used mainly, along with other tests, in people already diagnosed with a cancer that raises CEA — most commonly colorectal cancer: before treatment to help gauge severity (prognosis together with stage), during treatment to see whether CEA is falling, and after treatment to check whether cancer has come back. Depending on cancer type and stage, tests may be needed every 3–6 months during the first 5 years.

Physiology: CEA is a protein that helps cells divide quickly; healthy fetuses have high levels, which drop quickly after birth, so adults have very little if any. If CEA is present it may be a tumor marker; cancers that may raise it include those of the colon and rectum, prostate, ovary, lung, thyroid, liver, pancreas and breast.

slides.title: Carcinoembryonic antigen (CEA)
bullets: High: Non-cancer conditions can also raise CEA: gastritis and stomach ulcers, COPD, liver diseases (cirrhosis, gallstones, steatotic liver disease), diverticulitis, diabetes, and autoimmune or inflammatory diseases such as Crohn’s disease.

High: Before treatment, a low CEA may mean a small tumor that has not spread (though some cancers make little CEA), and a high CEA a larger tumor and/or spread — confirmed by other tests. During and after treatment, falling CEA often means treatment is working; rising or persistently high CEA may mean it is not (for example, after colorectal cancer surgery, that the tumor was not fully removed or is growing back); a fall followed by a rise may mean the cancer has come back.

slides.title: Carcinoembryonic antigen (CEA)
bullets: Pre-analytics: Usually no preparation is needed for a CEA blood test. If peritoneal fluid or cerebrospinal fluid is collected, you may be asked to empty your bladder and bowels; the sample is taken with a thin needle, with numbing medicine if needed.
Interferences: Smoking increases CEA, so people who smoke may be asked to stop for a while before the test.
Limitations: CEA tests are not used to screen for or diagnose cancer: results can be normal even with a cancer that can raise CEA, and many conditions that are not cancer can raise it.

CEA that stays high or rises after treatment does not always mean treatment is failing or cancer is growing — other tests are ordered to find out why. Labs use different methods to measure CEA, which affects results: to compare over time, have tests done the same way, usually in the same lab.

slides.title: Carcinoembryonic antigen (CEA)
bullets: General rule: circulating tumor markers have generally not worked well for screening people without symptoms — they miss some cancers (not sensitive enough) and can suggest cancer in people who do not have it (not specific enough). Non-cancer conditions can raise a marker, and some cancers do not raise it. A high marker only means cancer is more likely; a biopsy is usually needed to diagnose or rule out cancer.

slides.title: Alpha-fetoprotein (AFP) tumor marker
slides.eyebrow: Tumor markers · What it is used for · 1/2
bullets: Specimen: Venous blood

What it is used for: AFP is used with other tumor markers and imaging (ultrasound, CT, MRI) to monitor certain cancers and their treatment, help make a prognosis (how advanced the cancer is and how likely it is to respond), and check whether cancer has returned (AFP sometimes rises before symptoms). Per NCI, AFP helps diagnose liver cancer, ovarian cancer and germ cell tumors and is used to assess stage, prognosis and treatment response in germ cell tumors.

People with chronic hepatitis B or C or cirrhosis have a higher risk of liver cancer: AFP may be checked every six months with a liver ultrasound to help detect liver cancer early. A very high AFP or a sudden rise can be an early sign of liver cancer. The test is also ordered for symptoms of liver or germ cell cancers (belly pain or swelling, jaundice, a lump or swelling in a testicle).

slides.title: Alpha-fetoprotein (AFP) tumor marker
slides.eyebrow: Tumor markers · What it is used for · 2/2
bullets: Physiology: AFP is a protein the liver makes when its cells grow and divide. Levels are high in a fetus and drop very low after birth; healthy children and adults who are not pregnant have very little. Outside pregnancy AFP is mainly measured as a tumor marker: high AFP can be a sign of cancer of the liver (hepatocellular carcinoma), ovaries (germ cell tumors) or testicles (nonseminomatous germ cell tumors).

slides.title: Alpha-fetoprotein (AFP) tumor marker
bullets: High: AFP also rises in non-cancer liver conditions: cirrhosis, chronic hepatitis B or C, other liver disease and liver injury. Less often, high AFP comes with other cancers such as lymphoma or lung cancer. If there is no cancer diagnosis, the provider relies on medical history and other tests.

High: During treatment of a cancer that raised AFP: rising AFP may mean treatment is not working, falling AFP that it is, and unchanged AFP that the disease is stable. After treatment, AFP that is not normal may mean some cancer remains; higher than shortly after treatment may mean it is growing again. In chronic liver disease, a sudden rise or a very high AFP calls for other tests to check for liver cancer.

slides.title: Alpha-fetoprotein (AFP) tumor marker
bullets: Pre-analytics: No special preparation is needed; blood is drawn from a vein.

Limitations: High AFP does not always mean cancer, so an AFP result alone is not used to screen for or diagnose cancer. Some people with liver, ovarian or testicular cancer have normal AFP because not all tumors make it — a normal result does not rule out cancer.
The AFP test used in pregnancy is a different test: it also measures total AFP in blood, but it is not a tumor marker test — it checks the risk of certain birth defects in the fetus.

slides.title: Alpha-fetoprotein (AFP) tumor marker
bullets: General rule: circulating tumor markers have generally not worked well for screening people without symptoms — they miss some cancers (not sensitive enough) and can suggest cancer in people who do not have it (not specific enough). Non-cancer conditions can raise a marker, and some cancers do not raise it. A high marker only means cancer is more likely; a biopsy is usually needed to diagnose or rule out cancer.

slides.title: CA-125 (cancer antigen 125)
slides.eyebrow: Tumor markers · What it is used for · 1/2
bullets: Specimen: Venous blood

What it is used for: CA-125 is most often used to check whether ovarian cancer treatment is working or whether the cancer has come back. It also helps, with other tests, to learn whether a suspicious pelvic lump seen on imaging such as ultrasound could be ovarian cancer, and it may be suggested with other tests to screen women at very high risk.

Ovarian cancer risk may be high with: a mother or sister, or two or more other relatives, with ovarian cancer; family members with breast or colorectal cancer; changes in the BRCA1 or BRCA2 genes or inherited conditions such as Lynch syndrome; or a personal history of breast, uterine or colorectal cancer.

slides.title: CA-125 (cancer antigen 125)
slides.eyebrow: Tumor markers · What it is used for · 2/2
bullets: Physiology: CA-125 is a protein that acts as a tumor marker. Organs of the female reproductive system (ovaries, fallopian tubes) may make CA-125 when inflamed, including during normal functions such as a menstrual period. The body may also make high levels in response to ovarian cancer.

slides.title: CA-125 (cancer antigen 125)
bullets: High: Non-cancer conditions can also raise CA-125: endometriosis, pelvic inflammatory disease, uterine fibroids, liver disease, as well as natural processes such as menstrual periods and pregnancy.

High: During ovarian cancer treatment, CA-125 falling over several tests usually means treatment is helping; rising or unchanged levels may mean it is not working. After treatment, CA-125 rising over time may mean the cancer is coming back. In a woman at high risk or with a suspicious pelvic lump, a high CA-125 could be a sign of cancer, and more tests are ordered to make a diagnosis.

slides.title: CA-125 (cancer antigen 125)
bullets: Pre-analytics: No special preparation is needed; blood is drawn from a vein.

Limitations: CA-125 is not used to screen for ovarian cancer in women who are not at high risk, because non-cancer conditions also raise it. A normal CA-125 does not rule out cancer: it may be low in early stages, and not everyone with ovarian cancer has high levels. Only a biopsy can diagnose ovarian cancer.

After treatment for epithelial ovarian cancer, the most common type, the HE4 tumor marker may be tested along with CA-125: some studies show the two together give more accurate information about treatment response and recurrence.

slides.title: CA-125 (cancer antigen 125)
bullets: General rule: circulating tumor markers have generally not worked well for screening people without symptoms — they miss some cancers (not sensitive enough) and can suggest cancer in people who do not have it (not specific enough). Non-cancer conditions can raise a marker, and some cancers do not raise it. A high marker only means cancer is more likely; a biopsy is usually needed to diagnose or rule out cancer.

slides.title: CA 19-9 (cancer antigen 19-9)
slides.eyebrow: Tumor markers · What it is used for · 1/2
bullets: Specimen: Venous blood

What it is used for: CA 19-9 is used to monitor certain cancers and their treatment (it often rises as cancer grows and falls as tumors shrink), to help make a prognosis (stage and likelihood of responding to treatment), to check for recurrence after treatment (it often rises before other symptoms), and — only together with other tests — to check for certain cancers. NCI lists it for assessing whether treatment is working in pancreatic, gallbladder, bile duct and gastric cancers.

CA 19-9 is also ordered for symptoms of related cancers: jaundice, weight loss, belly pain, weakness, a swollen gallbladder or liver. When checking for signs of cancer, the provider also uses a physical exam, imaging (x-ray, CT, MRI) and cholangiopancreatography to see whether the pancreatic and bile ducts are narrowed or blocked.

slides.title: CA 19-9 (cancer antigen 19-9)
slides.eyebrow: Tumor markers · What it is used for · 2/2
bullets: Physiology: CA 19-9 is a protein that acts as a tumor marker. High levels can be a sign of certain cancers of the digestive tract and other organs: pancreas, bile duct, colon and rectum, stomach, ovaries and bladder.

slides.title: CA 19-9 (cancer antigen 19-9)
bullets: High: Non-cancer conditions can also raise CA 19-9: gallstones blocking the bile ducts, cholangitis (bile duct infection), pancreatitis, cirrhosis, bile duct disease, liver disease and cystic fibrosis. Healthy people without cancer can have high CA 19-9, and it does not always mean a problem that needs treatment.

High: During cancer treatment: rising CA 19-9 may mean the tumor is growing and/or treatment is not working; falling, that the tumor is shrinking and treatment is working; unchanged, that the disease is stable; a fall after treatment followed by a rise, that the cancer may have come back or grown. More tests are usually needed to know for sure.

slides.title: CA 19-9 (cancer antigen 19-9)
bullets: Pre-analytics: Usually no special preparation is needed, but check with the provider: if you take certain vitamins, you may need to stop them before the test.

Limitations: Because high CA 19-9 can mean different things, a CA 19-9 result alone is not used to screen for or diagnose cancer or other diseases. Some people do not make CA 19-9 even with a cancer that usually produces it — for them the test is not useful.

Labs use different methods to measure CA 19-9, and the method can affect the result. For regular cancer monitoring, have tests done the same way, usually in the same lab; the report usually states the method used.

slides.title: CA 19-9 (cancer antigen 19-9)
bullets: General rule: circulating tumor markers have generally not worked well for screening people without symptoms — they miss some cancers (not sensitive enough) and can suggest cancer in people who do not have it (not specific enough). Non-cancer conditions can raise a marker, and some cancers do not raise it. A high marker only means cancer is more likely; a biopsy is usually needed to diagnose or rule out cancer.

slides.title: Can CEA be used to screen healthy people without symptoms for colorectal cancer?
options: Yes, a normal CEA reliably rules out cancer and no other tests are needed
No, it is used mainly to monitor treatment and recurrence
slides.explanation:
Explanation: Correct. CEA tests are not used to screen for or diagnose cancer.

Basis: CEA can be normal with cancer and raised by non-cancer conditions.

slides.title: A man without symptoms has an elevated screening PSA. What is the usual next step per NCI?
options: Repeat the PSA in 6–8 weeks to confirm it
Diagnose prostate cancer and start treatment immediately without any further tests
slides.explanation:
Explanation: Correct. If it stays high — observation; if it keeps rising — further tests or a biopsy.

Basis: PSA can rise temporarily; the result is confirmed first, then observed or worked up.

slides.title: A woman with a suspicious pelvic lump has a normal CA-125. What does this mean?
options: Ovarian cancer is ruled out and no other tests are needed
Cancer is not ruled out: CA-125 can be low in early stages
slides.explanation:
Explanation: Correct. Not everyone with ovarian cancer has high CA-125; a biopsy makes the diagnosis.

Basis: CA-125 can be low early on; a biopsy makes the diagnosis.

slides.title: Which statement about AFP fits the source?
options: A high AFP always means liver cancer, so imaging and biopsy are unnecessary
It can also rise in cirrhosis and chronic hepatitis B/C
The pregnancy AFP test is also a tumor marker
slides.explanation:
Explanation: Correct. That is why AFP is used together with ultrasound and other tests.

Basis: AFP also rises in non-cancer liver disease and is not used alone for diagnosis.

slides.title: In which histological type of tumor are cells with round, oval, elongated hyperchromatic nuclei and signs of keratinization in the cytoplasm found in preparations:
Fundamentals of cytological examination. Importance of cytological examination in the diagnosis of neoplastic diseases?
bullets: 1. Cytology is making a diagnosis from the structure of cells: exfoliative (naturally shed or washing/brushing) and aspiration (fine needle aspirate) material.
2. Advantages: minimally invasive, rapid, inexpensive, repeatable; screening (cervix), early detection of tumors, assessing spread (fluids, lymph nodes), monitoring treatment effect.

3. Criteria of malignancy: nuclear enlargement and pleomorphism, increased N/C ratio, hyperchromasia and uneven chromatin, irregular nuclear membrane, prominent/multiple nucleoli, atypical mitoses, cell overlap and mutual "molding", loss of cohesion.
4. Limitations: does not show tissue architecture (invasion is hard to determine), specimen adequacy and reactive changes are sources of error; if needed, confirm with histology.

slides.title: Fundamentals of cytological examination. Importance of cytological examination in the diagnosis of neoplastic diseases?
bullets: 5. Additional methods: cell block, immunocytochemistry (for example TTF-1, p40, calretinin), molecular tests (HPV, mutations), liquid-based cytology.

slides.title: General information about tumors. Cytodiagnosis of malignant tumors?
bullets: 1. A tumor is a collection of clonal cells with uncontrolled proliferation; benign (mature, expansive growth, no metastasis) and malignant (immature, infiltrative growth, metastasis) tumors; epithelial (carcinomas), mesenchymal (sarcomas), hematopoietic (leukemias, lymphomas), etc.

2. Cytological signs of malignant tumors: cell and nuclear pleomorphism, increased N/C ratio, hyperchromasia, uneven chromatin, large/multiple nucleoli, atypical mitoses, loss of cohesion, necrotic background ("diathesis").

3. Signs of histogenetic type: squamous cell carcinoma (keratinization, "fiber" and "tadpole" cells), adenocarcinoma (glandular structures, vacuolated cytoplasm, eccentric nucleus), small cell carcinoma (small "molded" nuclei, scant cytoplasm), lymphoma (diffusely scattered monotonous lymphoid cells).

slides.title: General information about tumors. Cytodiagnosis of malignant tumors?
bullets: 4. Differentiation from reactive atypia (inflammation, regeneration, radiation) is a source of error; in doubtful cases the category "suspicious for malignancy" and histological confirmation.
5. Immunocytochemistry and molecular tests help to determine the origin of the tumor.

slides.title: Cytodiagnosis of tumors of the respiratory organs?
bullets: 1. Material: sputum (morning, several days), bronchial wash and brushing, bronchoalveolar lavage, transbronchial and EBUS-TBNA aspirates, pleural fluid.
2. Squamous cell carcinoma: keratinized, with dense orange cytoplasm (Pap), pleomorphic cells, hyperchromatic pyknotic nuclei; immunophenotype p40+.

3. Adenocarcinoma: groups and glandular/papillary structures, vacuolated cytoplasm, eccentric nuclei, prominent nucleoli; TTF-1 and Napsin-A positive; preserve material for molecular tests (EGFR, ALK, etc.).
4. Small cell carcinoma: small cells with scant cytoplasm, nuclei "molded" to each other, fine chromatin, crush artifact; neuroendocrine markers.
5. Sensitivity depends on the material and tumor location: for central tumors sputum and washings are more effective, for peripheral ones – guided aspiration; EBUS-TBNA in diagnosis and staging.

slides.title: Cytodiagnosis of tumors of the respiratory organs?
bullets: 6. Differentiation from reactive changes (metaplasia, regeneration, viruses).
